screens.body:
A unit is the smallest piece of code you can test on its own — usually one function. A unit test checks that one function, in isolation, does what it promises.

If add(2, 3) returns 5, the unit passes. If it returns 6, something's broken — and you know exactly where to look.
screens.heading: What is a unit?

screens.body:
An assertion is a statement you claim is true: "I expect add(2, 3) to equal 5." The test runner checks your claim.

If the assertion holds, the test passes. If it doesn't, the test fails loudly — and that's the point. Silent failures are how bugs ship.

options: Claims something is true and checks it
check.question: An assertion…

screens.heading: Assertions: the heart of every test
screens.keyPoint: Assert what you expect; let failures be loud.

screens.body:
Every unit test has the same skeleton. Arrange: set up inputs. Act: call the function. Assert: check the output.

This structure makes tests readable. Anyone — including future-you — can see what's being tested in seconds.
screens.heading: Arrange, Act, Assert in action
screens.keyPoint: Set up, do the thing, check the result.

screens.body:
What if your function calls a payment API? You don't want real charges in a test. So you use a test double — a fake stand-in.

A stub returns canned answers ("always say the payment succeeded"). A mock goes further: it records how it was called so you can verify the interaction. Both let you test YOUR code without the real dependency.

options: Returns canned answers instead of calling the real thing
check.question: A stub…

screens.heading: Test doubles: fakes on purpose
screens.keyPoint: Fake the dependency, test your code.

screens.body:
Each unit test should check exactly one thing. Not "does the cart work" — but "does adding an item increase the count" and separately "does the total update".

When a focused test fails, the failure message tells you what broke. When a giant test fails, you get to play detective.

options: A failure points straight at the broken behavior
check.question: Why one behavior per test?

screens.heading: One test, one behavior

screens.body:
Bugs love boundaries: empty strings, zero, negative numbers, the biggest possible value, null. These are edge cases.

A function that works for "normal" input and explodes on empty input isn't done. Great unit tests deliberately poke the edges.

options: Boundary inputs like empty, zero, or max values
check.question: Edge cases are…

code.snippet:
// edge cases for a discount function
discount(100, 0);   // 0% off
discount(100, 100); // 100% off — free?
discount(0, 10);    // $0 item

screens.heading: Edge cases: where bugs hide
screens.keyPoint: Test the boundaries, not just the middle.

screens.body:
Your escrow dApp moves money: release payment, refund buyer. Those are pure functions — perfect unit test targets.

Before that demo ever touches real funds, unit tests prove the math: correct split, correct refund, no rounding that leaks cents. That's what makes a reviewer trust your code.

options: It's pure logic — easy to test in isolation
check.question: Escrow math is a great unit-test target because…

screens.heading: Why this matters for you
screens.keyPoint: Unit-test the money math before it touches real funds.
